Large Language Models as Annotators for Machine Translation Quality
Estimation
Sidi Wang
Maastricht university
sidi.wang@
maastrichtuniversity.nlSophie Arnoult
Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
s.i.arnoult@vu.nlAmir Kamran
Taus
amir@taus.net
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demon-
strated excellent performance on Machine Trans-
lation Quality Estimation (MTQE), yet their high
inference costs make them impractical for direct ap-
plication. In this work, we propose applying LLMs
to generate MQM-style annotations for training a
COMET model: following Fernandes et al. (2023),
we reckon that segment-level annotations provide
a strong rationale for LLMs and are key to good
segment-level QE. We propose a simplified MQM
scheme, mostly restricted to top-level categories,
to guide LLM selection. We present a systematic
approach for the development of a GPT-4o-based
prompt, called PPbMQM (Prompt-Pattern-based-
MQM). We show that the resulting annotations
correlate well with human annotations and that
training COMET on them leads to competitive per-
formance on segment-level QE for Chinese-English
and English-German.
1 Introduction
Machine Translation (MT) Quality Estimation
(QE) metrics fine-tuned on human judgement data
like CometKIWI (Rei et al., 2022, 2023) now per-
form on-par with reference-based metrics (Freitag
et al., 2021b, 2022, 2023, 2024; Lavie et al., 2025).
Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT
(Brown et al., 2020) and PaLM (Chowdhery
et al., 2023; Anil et al., 2023) exhibit human-
level performance on various benchmark NLP
tasks (Huang and Chang, 2023). Kocmi and Fe-
dermann (2023b) were the first to utilize LLM
prompting for QE, prompting GPT models to out-
put Direct-Assessment (DA) scores. Their GPT-
4-based metric GEMBA showing state-of-the-art
performance at the system level, where QE metrics
have to rank (test)set outputs of translation systems,
and promising results at the segment level, wherescores are assigned to sentence translations.
Fernandes et al. (2023) prompt PaLM mod-
els to output Multidimensional Quality Metric
(MQM) annotations (Burchardt, 2013; Lommel
et al., 2014), which mark error spans in translations
with a type and degree of severity, as shown in Fig-
ure 1, and have been introduced in the WMT eval-
uation campaigns following Freitag et al. (2021a).
Prompting for MQM provides interpretable results
and also triggers reasoning in LLMs, and Fernan-
des et al. (2023) show that their few-shot AU-
TOMQM prompt has high recall on major errors
and improved segment-level predictions with the
larger PaLM-2 Unicorn model (Anil et al., 2023)
compared to DA-score prompting.
Figure 1: Example MQM annotation. Error spans are
marked with error type and severity.
MQM annotations remain hard to operational-
ize, and other QE studies have proposed to iden-
tify error spans with their severity only and not
with the error types (Perrella et al., 2022; Lu et al.,
2023; Rei et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2024; Kocmi
et al., 2024b), as the scores required for training
QE learned metrics are obtained by weighing errors
based on their severity, but also because it is suffi-
cient for post-editing tasks (Kocmi and Federmann,
2023a; Zouhar et al., 2024). This also has resulted
in the recent replacement of MQM by ESA (Kocmi
et al., 2024b) in the WMT General Machine Trans-
lation shared task (Kocmi et al., 2024a). Rather
than discarding all category information, we sim-
plify the MQM scheme to top-level categories, and
adding theOmissionsubcategory, which allows us
to analyse the error types made by different LLMs.
Inference with LLMs is slow and costly (ReiarXiv:2603.10775v1  [cs.CL]  11 Mar 2026

et al., 2023), therefore we propose to use LLMs
to generatesynthetic MQM-style annotations for
finetuning learned metrics. We make the following
contributions:
•We introduce a few-shot PPbMQM prompt,
restricted to the top-level MQM categories for
error type and theomissioncategory.
•Our analysis on Chinese-English confirms
that LLMs are overly critical; we show that
prompting along a severity scale as a basis for
score computation improves correlation with
human judgments.
•We apply our prompt to generating training
data for COMET-QE1for Chinese-English
and English-German, showing positive results
with Pearson correlation compared to human
annotations.
2 Prompt development for MQM
2.1 Experiment design
We develop our prompt in four steps: 1) testing
LLMs on their knowledge of QE and MQM; 2)
identifying issues with a first zero-shot prompt; 3)
zero-shot prompting; 4) few-shot prompting. The
first three steps are presented in section 2.2, and
few-shot prompting in section 2.3.
The MQM annotation scheme employs a refined
hierarchical error typology. To simplify the task
for LLMs, we initially restricted ourselves to the
top-level MQM categoriesAccuracy,Fluency,Ter-
minology,Style, andLocale Convention–adding the
subcategoryOmissionfor few-shot experiments–
and to two severity levels,MajorandMinor.
Following White et al. (2023), we apply theper-
sonaand thereflectionpatterns to elicit better in-
formed predictions, and theoutput automaterpat-
tern for structured output. The rationale details can
be found in Appendix A.1.
We experimented with four large LLMs, GPT-
3.5, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, and LLaMA 3 70B2
on Chinese-English, selecting the best performing
models after each step.
Our dataset is from the Chinese-English and
English-German Expert-Based Human Evaluations
(EbHE-WMT-MT) of the 2022 and 2023 WMT
general MT task (Freitag et al., 2021a).
1GitHub:https://github.com/Unbabel/COMET
2We used APIs provided by OpenAI and Replicate.2.2 Zero-shot prompting
We first tested the translation knowledge of the
four LLMs by asking questions related to QE and
MQM, and scoring answers on a scale of 1 to 5.
GPT-3.5 performed the poorest, scoring 14 out of
25, compared to 19 or 20 for the other models
(see Table 1), and was then excluded from further
analysis.
Secondly, we designed a zero-shot prompt that
relies on LLMs’ inherent knowledge of MQM,
shown in Figure 2. Testing this prompt on 10
[System message]You are a professional
Chinese-English translator.
[Instruction message]Your task is to identify
translation errors from a pair of the source
Chinese sentence and the target English sentence.
Please identify up to 5 errors and assign an
error type for each with a severity label from
"major" and "minor", using the MQM annotation
scheme. Please provide the output only in json
format: 1. error type (value scope: accuracy,
style, fluency, terminology, locale convention,
other) 2. marked text (the identified error in
the target sentence) 3. error span index (split
the target sentence with whitespace and get the
marked text start and end index) 4. severity (major
or minor) 5. explanation.
Figure 2: Initial zero-shot prompt. This prompt was
further developed by changing the error span index in-
struction into ‘split the target sentence using NLTK
tokenizer and get the marked text start and end index’.
segments showed that all three LLMs provided
clear and readable values for the required fields, but
generated inconsistent indices. We solved this by
choosing the span closest to the indices in the case
of ties. We also modified the prompt to tokenize
with the NLTK tokenizer instead of by whitespace.
Thirdly, we applied the revised prompt to all
three models, evaluating generated annotations
against human annotations on span metrics (span,
severity, and error-type F1), which are calculated
following Blain et al. (2023), and on correlation to
quality scores, which are derived from MQM anno-
tations by weighing major/minor errors by 5 and 1,
respectively, following Freitag et al. (2021a).
Results are presented in Table 2. Not all models
are equally capable of producing parsable annota-
tions: only 70% of the GPT-4 Turbo annotations
were parsable, compared to around 90% for GPT-
4o and LLaMA 3. For these two models–although

use of the future tense as incorrect, although the ex-
act tense of the source sentence was unclear since
tense is unmarked in Chinese. In many if not most
cases, LLMs are more sensitive to subtle errors
than human annotators. For instance, in the seg-
ment pair 电池在用。 / The battery is working,
GPT-4o markedworkingas a major accuracy error,
which is correct considering that 在用 meansin use;
in the segment pair 防骗提示： / Anti-fraud tips:,
GPT-4 Turbo flagged a minor accuracy error, which
is correct considering that a better translation might

beFraud prevention tips.
Error-typing scores are low: among the most fre-
quent error types identified by humans (Accuracy,
Style,Fluency),StyleandFluencywere misclas-
sified the most (see Table 4). The comma splice
Fluencyerror is among the most common errors.
We used this to inform few-shot prompting.
While LLaMA 3 annotations correlate the best
with human annotations3, we found its API stabil-
ity to be lower than that of GPT-4o, experiencing
multiple interruptions and errors when handling
batch requests. We therefore selected GPT-4o for
few-shot prompting and QE model training4.
2.3 Few-shot prompting
At this step, we improved our prompt by adding:
1) detailed explanations for each error type; 2) an
example ofOmission, as we discovered that GPT-
4o did not identify this error type in the zero-shot
setting5; 3) an example of comma spliceFluency
error. Furthermore, to emulate human annotator
behavior, we devised a new method for severity
classification: instead ofmajor/minorlabels, we
prompt for a severity score on a scale of1-5and
then map the score ranges 4-5 toMajorand ranges
1-3 toMinor. The final prompt version is shown in
Appendix figure 3.
Results are presented in Table 2. Few-shot PPb-
MQM leads to improved span metrics for GPT-4o6,
but not directly to improved correlation with hu-
man annotations. However, a severity scale allows
us to set a threshold for minor errors.
We tested different score-to-category mappings
and obtained the best result by discarding anno-
tations with severity scores 1-2, mapping only
severity-3 scores to theminorcategory. We use
our few-shot PPbMQM prompt with this mapping
to generate annotations and derive quality scores
for QE model training.
3This may seem contradictory given the lower span scores
compared to GPT-4o, but correlations are calculated based on
error numbers and severity labels in each segment, regardless
of the span accuracy.
4We conducted stability analyses on GPT-4o with a basic
prompt variant and different system_fingerprint values rep-
resenting the backend models. Both analyses demonstrated
stable behavior (see Appendix A.3 for results).
5According to the MQM typology ( https://themqm.

We annotated 20703 zh-en and 10121 en-de seg-
ments by applying PPbMQM7. For each language
pair, we trained two reference-free QE models
with COMET using default settings, one using
PPbMQM-generated annotations and a baseline
using human MQM annotations. We then tested
both models on randomly selected segments.
As Table 5 shows, for both languague pairs, the
QE models trained on PPbMQM annotations per-
forms on par with the models trained on human
annotations, achieving higher Pearson correlation
scores than the baseline models, albeit lower Spear-
man and Kendall τ. In the lower quality segments,
which represent a quarter of the data, they outper-
form the human-data trained models in all metrics.
This might be related to low inter-annotator agree-
ment for fine-grained linguistic tasks like MQM
annotations8: the more consistent LLM annota-
tions may be better exploited by COMET, and the
difference can best be seen in segments with more
errors.
4 Discussion
We have presented a stepwise prompting approach
that progresses from knowledge testing of LLMs
to zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Our pri-
mary motivation in developing a new MQM-based
prompt was not to outperform existing prompting
methods, but to provide a systematic and compre-
hensive approach that integrates prompting with
downstream QE-model training. We believe that
our proposed scheme is also informative for quality
evaluation with the ESA protocol (Kocmi et al.,
2024b).
Our approach and findings complement earlier
work on MQM-related annotations for Quality Es-
timation: we redefined key error categories to bal-
ance informativeness and simplicity, keeping a sub-
set of the MQM typology; we found, like Fernan-
des et al. (2023) and Zouhar et al. (2024), that
LLMs tend to overpredict errors, and we introduced
a severity scaling method to effectively control their
number; we did not experiment with the number
of few-shot examples (Fernandes et al., 2023; Rei

Our prompting method generates annotations
that correlate well with human annotations and that
can serve for training learned QE metrics. While
experimenting with more language pairs is neces-
sary, this opens up the way to training QE mod-
els for language pairs that do not yet benefit from
MQM reference annotations. As Chinese-English
and English-German are high-resource language
pairs, it would be interesting, in particular, to see
how LLMs perform when prompted for other lower-
resource language pairs.
The COMET model trained on our synthetic data
achieved better correlation with the reference an-
notations in the lower-quality segments. Although
this was not the focus of this work, this result is par-
ticularly relevant for automated post-editing (Zerva
et al., 2024).
5 Conclusion
We have presented an MQM-based prompt for gen-
erating synthetic data for QE learned-metrics train-
ing. We keep a subset of the MQM error types and
address the sensitivity of LLMs to translation errors
with a severity scale, discarding low-severity errors.
Our synthetic annotations lead to competitive per-
formance for COMET on both Chinese-English
and English-German. In future work, we plan to
extend this approach to more language pairs.Limitations
Our test and development datasets may have been
included in the training data of LLMs, causing data
leakage issues.
The training data used for our downstream QE
model training experiment only covered two lan-
guage pairs on news, e-commerce, conversation,
and social media domains, thus it might fail to
handle tasks from other domains or/and language
pairs.
Our COMET-framework-based QE models were
trained with only one initialization. Future efforts
should be made to test on models with multiple
initializations to obtain a sufficient sample for the
statistical test, strengthening the experimental evi-
dence (Ulmer et al., 2022).
Ethics Statement
We used proprietary LLMs for which the source of
the training data is unknown.

A Appendix
A.1 Basic prompt design
Three prompt patterns from White et al. (2023) are used for our basic prompt design:
1) The persona pattern:You are a professional Chinese-English translator.
This statement asks LLM to act as a specific persona – in this case, a Chinese-English translator for our
task, which should evoke traits associated with the persona.
2) The output automater pattern:Please output a json file with the following keys; Please only
generate in json format
These two statements ask the LLM to provide the output in JSON format, constraining the structure of the
output. If the LLM follows the instructions and produces the JSON pattern output, the manual editing
effort can be reduced for automatic evaluation. Additional instructions are also given for each key to
obtain output with a standard vocabulary for MQM annotations.
3) The reflection pattern:Please provide an explanation for the generated output
Asking LLMs to produce an explanation for each identified error can help us understand the reasoning
and assumption behind it.
Furthermore, the phraseusing the MQM annotation schemeis added to elicit more domain
knowledge that could possibly be acquired during the training phase.

A.2 Few-shot prompt
[System message] You are a professional Chinese-English translator.
[Instruction message] You are a professional Chinese-English translator. Your
task is to identify translation errors from a pair of the source Chinese sentence and
the target English sentence. Please identify a maximum of 5 errors, assigning an error
type for each with a severity scale from 1 (least severe) to 5 (most severe) using the
MQM annotation scheme. Please consider the following criteria for identifying errors:
Accuracy: when the target translation does not accurately represent the source.
Omission: when the target translation is missing content present in the source text.
Identify if any information has been omitted.
Fluency: issues with punctuation, spelling, grammar, register, inconsistency.
Style: when the translation is grammatically correct but uses unnatural or awkward
language.
Terminology: inappropriate or inconsistent use of terms.
Locale convention: issues with formatting.
Please provide the output in JSON format including the following keys for
each error: [“error type” (value: accuracy, omission, style, fluency, terminology,
locale convention, other), “error span index” (start and end index of the marked
text in the target sentence), “marked text” (the identified error in the target
sentence), “severity”: (1-5)]

structure.title: Introduction
structure.summary:
This document proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate annotations for Machine Translation Quality Estimation (MTQE). The authors acknowledge that while LLMs perform well on MTQE, their high inference costs make them impractical for direct use. To address this, they suggest using LLMs to create MQM-style annotations for training a COMET model.

Key points covered include:

*   **Problem:** High inference costs of LLMs for direct MTQE application.
*   **Proposed Solution:** Use LLMs to generate MQM-style annotations for training MTQE models.
*   **Methodology:**
    *   Propose a simplified MQM scheme, focusing on top-level categories and an "omission" subcategory.
    *   Develop a systematic approach for creating a GPT-4o-based prompt called PPbMQM (Prompt-Pattern-based-MQM).
    *   Employ a four-step prompt development process: testing LLM knowledge, identifying issues with a zero-shot prompt, refining zero-shot prompting, and finally, few-shot prompting.
    *   Utilize persona, reflection, and output automater patterns to elicit better predictions and structured output.
    *   Experiment with different LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, LLaMA 3 70B2) and a dataset from WMT general MT tasks.
*   **Findings/Contributions:**
    *   The generated annotations correlate well with human annotations.
    *   Training COMET on these synthetic annotations leads to competitive performance on segment-level QE for Chinese-English and English-German.
    *   Analysis shows LLMs can be overly critical, and prompting along a severity scale improves correlation with human judgments.
    *   The PPbMQM prompt is introduced, restricted to top-level MQM categories and the omission subcategory.

structure.title: Prompt development for MQM
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a research proposal to use Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate synthetic MQM-style annotations for finetuning learned metrics. The main points covered are:

*   **Contributions:**
    *   Introduction of a few-shot prompt (PPbMQM) restricted to top-level MQM categories and an "omission" category.
    *   Analysis confirming LLMs are overly critical and that prompting with a severity scale improves correlation with human judgments.
    *   Application of the prompt to generate training data for COMET-QE1 on Chinese-English and English-German, showing positive results.

*   **Prompt Development for MQM:**
    *   **Experiment Design:** A four-step process involving testing LLM knowledge, identifying issues with zero-shot prompts, and then developing zero-shot and few-shot prompts.
    *   **MQM Annotation Scheme Simplification:** Restriction to top-level MQM categories (Accuracy, Fluency, Terminology, Style, Locale Convention, Omission) and two severity levels (Major, Minor) for LLMs.
    *   **Prompting Patterns:** Use of "persona" and "reflection" patterns for better predictions and "output automater" for structured output.
    *   **LLM Experimentation:** Testing GPT-3.5, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, and LLaMA 3 70B on Chinese-English data.
    *   **Dataset:** Chinese-English and English-German Expert-Based Human Evaluations (EbHE-WMT-MT) from WMT general MT tasks.
    *   **Zero-shot Prompting:**
        *   Initial testing of LLM knowledge of QE and MQM, excluding GPT-3.5 due to poor performance.
        *   Design of an initial zero-shot prompt (shown in Figure 2) and identification of issues with inconsistent indices, which were addressed by choosing the closest span and modifying tokenization.
        *   Evaluation of revised zero-shot prompts against human annotations using span metrics and correlation to quality scores.
        *   Results indicating varying parsability of annotations across LLMs, with GPT-4o and LLaMA 3 showing higher parsability.

nodes.title: Zero-shot prompting
nodes.summary:
This document proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate synthetic MQM-style annotations for fine-tuning learned metrics, specifically for machine translation quality estimation. The main points covered are:

*   **Contributions:**
    *   Introduction of a few-shot PPbMQM prompt, limited to top-level MQM categories and an "omission" subcategory.
    *   Analysis confirming LLMs are overly critical, and that prompting with a severity scale improves correlation with human judgments.
    *   Application of the prompt to generate training data for COMET-QE1 on Chinese-English and English-German, showing positive results.

*   **Prompt Development for MQM:**
    *   **Experiment Design:** A four-step process involving testing LLM knowledge, identifying issues with zero-shot prompts, developing zero-shot prompts, and then few-shot prompts.
    *   **MQM Scheme Simplification:** Restriction to top-level MQM categories (Accuracy, Fluency, Terminology, Style, Locale Convention, Omission) and two severity levels (Major, Minor) for LLMs.
    *   **LLM Selection:** Experimentation with GPT-3.5, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4o, and LLaMA 3 70B.
    *   **Dataset:** Chinese-English and English-German Expert-Based Human Evaluations (EbHE-WMT-MT) from WMT.
    *   **Zero-shot Prompting:** Initial testing of LLM knowledge, design of a zero-shot prompt, identification of issues with index generation, and evaluation against human annotations using span metrics and correlation to quality scores. Results showed GPT-4o and LLaMA 3 were more capable of producing parsable annotations than GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 Turbo. LLMs were found to be stricter than human annotators.
    *   **Few-shot Prompting:** Improvement of the prompt by adding detailed explanations, an example of "Omission," and an example of a "comma splice Fluency" error. A severity scale (1-5) was introduced, mapping to Major/Minor labels. This led to improved span metrics but not directly improved correlation with human annotations. A specific mapping of severity scores to categories was found to be optimal.

*   **Downstream QE Model Training:**
    *   Annotation of a large number of Chinese-English and English-German segments using PPbMQM.
    *   Training of reference-free QE models with COMET using both PPbMQM-generated annotations and human MQM annotations.
    *   Results showed that QE models trained on PPbMQM annotations performed comparably to those trained on human annotations, outperforming them in lower quality segments. This is attributed to potentially more consistent LLM annotations.

*   **Discussion:**
    *   The proposed stepwise prompting approach integrates prompting with downstream QE model training.
    *   The scheme is informative for quality evaluation with the ESA protocol.
    *   The work complements previous research by redefining error categories, confirming LLMs' tendency to overpredict errors, and introducing a severity scaling method.

nodes.title: Few-shot prompting
nodes.summary:
This document describes a method for generating synthetic data for training Quality Estimation (QE) models using Large Language Models (LLMs). The approach involves a stepwise prompting strategy, starting with basic prompts and progressing to few-shot prompting. Key aspects covered include:

*   **Error Identification and Classification:** The document discusses the challenges of LLMs misclassifying error types like "Style" and "Fluency," and how specific errors like comma splices were identified.
*   **LLM Selection:** GPT-4o was chosen over LLaMA 3 for its API stability, despite LLaMA 3 showing better correlation with human annotations.
*   **Few-Shot Prompting Enhancement:** The prompt was improved by adding detailed explanations for error types, examples of specific errors (Omission, comma splice Fluency error), and a severity scale (1-5) to better emulate human annotator behavior.
*   **Severity Scaling and Mapping:** A method for mapping severity scores to "Major" and "Minor" labels was developed, and specific score ranges were found to be optimal for discarding low-severity errors.
*   **Downstream QE Model Training:** The generated synthetic annotations (PPbMQM) were used to train reference-free QE models using COMET.
*   **Performance Comparison:** QE models trained on synthetic data performed comparably to those trained on human annotations, particularly excelling in lower-quality segments. This is attributed to the potential consistency of LLM annotations compared to human inter-annotator agreement.
*   **Discussion and Limitations:** The document highlights the systematic nature of their prompting approach, its potential for low-resource language pairs, and its relevance for automated post-editing. Limitations include potential data leakage and the limited scope of domains and language pairs tested.
*   **Ethics Statement:** The use of proprietary LLMs with unknown training data sources is acknowledged.
*   **Appendix:** Details on the basic prompt design, including persona, output automation, and reflection patterns, are provided.

(2023): the persona pattern (instructing the LLM to act as a professional Chinese-English translator), the output automater pattern (requiring JSON output with specific keys for reduced manual editing and automatic evaluation), and the reflection pattern (asking for explanations of generated outputs to understand reasoning). The document also mentions the inclusion of the phrase "using the MQM annotation scheme" to encourage domain-specific knowledge.

nodes.title: Basic prompt design
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes prompt design strategies for a Chinese-English translation task, focusing on improving the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs). It details two main prompt design approaches:

**A.1 Basic Prompt Design:** This section outlines three fundamental prompt patterns adapted from White et al. (2023):
*   **Persona Pattern:** Instructs the LLM to adopt a specific role (e.g., a professional Chinese-English translator) to elicit relevant traits.
*   **Output Automater Pattern:** Guides the LLM to produce output in a structured format, specifically JSON, to facilitate automatic evaluation and reduce manual editing. It also mentions adding instructions for specific keys to ensure standardized vocabulary for MQM annotations.
*   **Reflection Pattern:** Prompts the LLM to provide explanations for its generated output, aiding in understanding its reasoning and assumptions.
The section also notes the addition of the phrase "using the MQM annotation scheme" to encourage the LLM to leverage domain knowledge.

**A.2 Few-Shot Prompt:** This section presents an improved prompt design that incorporates few-shot learning. It includes:
*   A system message and an instruction message that clearly define the LLM's role, task, and constraints.
*   Specific error categories (Accuracy, Omission, Fluency, Style, Terminology, Locale Convention) with detailed criteria for identification.
*   A severity scale (1-5) for rating errors.
*   A requirement for JSON output with specific keys: "error type", "error span index", "marked text", and "severity".
*   Examples of source-target sentence pairs with identified errors, demonstrating the application of the prompt and the expected output format.
*   A reference to Figure 3, which highlights improvements made to the prompt, including the severity scale, detailed error explanations, and examples for specific error types like Fluency and Omission.

nodes.title: Few-shot prompt
nodes.summary: This partial document describes a "few-shot prompt" designed for a Chinese-English translator. The prompt instructs the translator to identify translation errors in a given source Chinese sentence and target English sentence pair. It specifies a maximum of 5 errors to be identified, each with an assigned error type (accuracy, omission, fluency, style, terminology, locale convention, or other) and a severity scale from 1 (least severe) to 5 (most severe) using the MQM annotation scheme. The document also lists criteria for identifying errors, including accuracy, omission, fluency, style, terminology, locale convention, and provides examples of how these errors should be marked and formatted in a JSON output. Figure 3 is referenced, highlighting improvements made to the prompt compared to a "zero-shot prompt," specifically mentioning the inclusion of a severity scale, detailed error category explanations, and examples of fluency and omission errors.

nodes.title: Stability analysis
nodes.summary: This partial document section, titled "A.3 Stability analysis," presents results from two stability tests. Table 6 details zero-shot performance metrics for "basic prompt" and "prompt variant" using GPT-4o with 400 output segments, focusing on span, severity, and error type F1 scores, as well as Pearson and Spearman correlations. Table 7 shows a fingerprint analysis on a QE-training dataset generated by PPbMQM, also reporting span, severity, and error type F1 scores, along with Pearson and Spearman correlations for different system fingerprints.
